lessons.title: Understand the Market
body: Before you build anything, you need a market worth serving — a specific group of people with a real problem, the money to pay for a solution, and a way for you to actually reach them. Most beginners start with a skill (“I'm good at teaching Arabic” or “I know how to design logos”) and try to find customers afterward. This module reverses that: you investigate demand first, so the thing you eventually build already has somewhere to land.

These three words get used interchangeably, and that's where a lot of beginners go wrong. Your audience is whoever already pays attention to you — followers, students, past clients. Your niche is a specific slice of a broader field, defined by a shared interest or problem — not “fitness,” but “beginners who want to work out at home with no equipment.” Your market is the part of that niche that's both willing and able to pay for a solution right now. A content creator might have ten thousand followers (a sizeable audience) interested in productivity (a broad field), but only a fraction of them are actively searching for and willing to pay for a specific productivity tool (the market). You're not building for your audience or your niche — you're building for your market.

Skipping this step is the single most common reason a first digital product doesn't sell: the creator built something they personally thought was useful, for a customer they imagined rather than one they'd actually found talking about the problem. Everything in this module exists to replace that imagined customer with a real, evidenced one.

DigitalOps evaluates a candidate market on four signals, together called the Market Pulse Check, shown below. Lesson 1.2 teaches you exactly how to go find real evidence for each one; Lesson 1.3 teaches you how to turn that evidence into an honest score.

A quick, hypothetical sense of what each signal looks like before you dig in — none of this is real research, just illustration: a private tutor notices the same question asked repeatedly in a parenting forum — that's Hunger. A freelance designer finds founders already paying thousands of dollars for branding work — that's Wallet. A fitness coach finds an active, searchable community of home-workout beginners — that's Reach. A content creator notices a wave of new accounts asking about a tool that barely existed two years ago — that's Momentum. Lesson 1.2 shows you how to go find your own evidence like this.
lessons.insight: A market can be real and still be wrong for you if it fails even one signal — genuine pain with no spending power, or spending power you can't reach, both kill an otherwise good idea.

lessons.title: Research the Market
body: This is the practical core of Module 1: exactly where to look for evidence of a real market, what to search for, and how to tell a genuine problem from idle curiosity. Everything below uses short, hypothetical examples from a few different niches — an Arabic teacher, a freelance designer, a fitness coach, a private tutor, a content creator — purely to illustrate the method. They are not real research or verified market data; the principles transfer to whatever your own expertise is.

Where to research
  • Threads and niche forums. Most established hobbies and professions still have a dedicated forum or discussion board. Use the forum's own search for your topic, then read the oldest unresolved threads — those are problems nobody has solved well yet.
  • Reddit. Search a relevant subreddit, or use a web search like site:reddit.com [your niche] “how do I”. A freelance designer researching branding might search r/smallbusiness or r/entrepreneur for “logo” or “brand identity” — look for the same question asked by different people over months, not once.
  • X / Twitter. Use the platform's own search for phrases like “I wish there was” or “does anyone know a tool for” plus your niche keyword. Its advanced search can filter by date, which helps you see whether a complaint is recent or has been going on for years.
  • Facebook Groups. Join two or three groups in your niche and use each group's internal search. A fitness coach researching home workouts might search “no equipment” inside a beginner-fitness group and read every comment on the most-replied posts.
  • Discord and Slack communities. Harder to search from outside, but once you're a member, the #help or #questions channel is often the richest source of real-time, specific problems — read a week of history rather than guessing from the channel name.
  • Quora. Search your topic directly (“how to learn Arabic as an adult beginner”). Questions are often worded exactly how a real customer would ask — useful later for naming and positioning too.
  • YouTube comments. Find the two or three most-watched videos on your topic and read the comments, not the video. A content creator researching a note-taking guide might watch top “how I study” videos and look for comments like “what's the best way to organize notes digitally.”
  • Amazon reviews. Search for an adjacent physical or Kindle product and sort by lowest-rated — one- and two-star reviews tell you exactly what a solution needs to do that the existing one doesn't.
  • App Store and software reviews. Same idea, applied to apps. Open the closest competing app and read its low-star reviews for specific missing features or complaints.
  • Gumroad and other digital-product marketplaces. Search your topic directly — what's already selling, at what price, and what do its reviews say is missing? A private tutor researching learning resources might note three similar products' prices as a future pricing anchor too (useful again in Module 5).
  • Freelance marketplaces and job listings. Search job posts on Upwork, Fiverr, or similar. A paid post (“looking for someone to redesign my logo, budget $500”) is about as strong a buying signal as you can find before you've launched anything.

No two platforms search the same way — some have a strong internal search, others are better searched through a general search engine with a site: filter. Whichever platform you're on, replace generic phrases with your own niche's words: “How do I…”, “I'm struggling with…”, “Is there a tool that…”, “What's the best way to…”, “I wish there was…”, “Does anyone recommend…”, “I'm currently paying for…”, “Where can I buy…”. Each tends to surface a different kind of evidence — the next section explains which.

Telling curiosity from buying intent
Not every mention of a problem means someone will pay to solve it. As you read, sort what you find into four levels, weakest to strongest: general curiosity (“I wish someone would make a tool for this” — a passing wish, no real pressure behind it); a person experiencing a problem (“I've tried three different tools, but none of them solve this properly” — real frustration, actively comparing options); a person actively searching for a solution (“does anyone know where I can buy a solution for this?” — asking specifically to be sold to); and a person already spending money to solve it — already paying for an imperfect alternative, already paying someone to do it manually, or visibly spending significant time on a workaround. The further down this list your evidence sits, the stronger it is. A single comment at the curiosity level proves almost nothing on its own; a pattern of comments at the third or fourth level, from different people, is real signal.

Recording what you find
Don't rely on memory or a folder of random screenshots — log each piece of evidence the same way, so you can compare entries later. For every discussion worth noting, record: date you found it; platform or source; link to the public discussion; the customer's statement, quoted or closely paraphrased; the problem it points to; any existing solution or workaround they mention; evidence of willingness to pay, if any; and which Market Pulse signal it supports. A simple spreadsheet with these eight columns works fine. Once you have ten or fifteen entries, look across them for the same problem showing up from independent people on different platforms — that repetition, not any single entry, is what tells you a market is real.

A few rules
Don't treat one comment as proof of demand — look for the pattern. Don't invent customer evidence to fill out your log; an empty row is more honest than a fabricated one and tells you to keep researching. Use only publicly accessible information — don't scrape private communities, and if you ever message someone directly to ask questions, be upfront about who you are and get their OK first. Keep a clear line between what you observed (someone wrote this exact sentence) and what you're assuming (you think this means they'd pay $50) — write both down, but label them differently in your log.
lessons.insight: A pattern across five strangers on three different platforms is worth more than one glowing comment from someone you know — independence and repetition are what make evidence real.

lessons.title: Evaluate the Market
body: You've gathered evidence. Now you need to turn it into an honest score on each of the four Market Pulse signals — not a guess, and not a perfect science either. This lesson shows what a low, medium, and high score actually looks like for each signal, so the sliders in your exercise reflect what you found, not a feeling.

Hunger — how strong is the problem?
Low

you found one or two mentions, phrased as mild curiosity, with no repetition across sources.

Medium

the same complaint from several people, but phrased mildly — annoyance, not urgency.

High

multiple independent people describe real frustration or mention actively trying (and failing) to solve it themselves — for example, a hypothetical Arabic teacher finding the same “I keep forgetting the alphabet within a week” complaint repeated across five different language-learning forum threads.

Common mistake: scoring Hunger high because the topic is popular, not because the problem itself is painful — a big audience talking casually about a topic isn't the same as that audience hurting over a specific problem.

Wallet — can this audience pay?
Low

no evidence of existing spending anywhere in your log, and the audience skews toward free alternatives.

Medium

some evidence of spending, but on cheap alternatives, or clearly reluctant.

High

people already paying a meaningful amount for an imperfect alternative, or paying someone directly to solve the problem manually — for example, a hypothetical freelance designer finding founders already paying $2,000–$5,000 for branding work elsewhere.

Common mistake: assuming a market can pay because the audience is large, or because you personally would pay — check your log for actual spending evidence, not inference.

Reach — can you find and talk to them?
Low

your evidence came from scattered, hard-to-access, or private sources you can't realistically post in or reach again.

Medium

a few accessible venues, but small, or you have no existing presence there.

High

active, open communities with real volume, where you could realistically post or run a small test — for example, a hypothetical fitness coach finding three active, large communities specifically for home workouts.

Common mistake: confusing “this market exists” with “I can reach this market” — a real audience you have no way to reach yet scores low on Reach, regardless of the other three signals.

Momentum — is demand stable, emerging or growing?
Low

the discussions you found are old, infrequent, or clearly declining.

Medium

steady, consistent mentions over time, with no clear growth or decline.

High

new discussions, new accounts, or new questions appearing more often than they used to — for example, a hypothetical content creator noticing a wave of new posts about a tool or trend that barely existed two years ago.

Common mistake: mistaking one viral post or a short-lived spike for real momentum — check whether interest is sustained over weeks or months, not just one busy week.

Deciding what to do with your scores
The Market Pulse Check is a directional decision-making tool, not a statistically validated predictor of sales — there's no universal passing score that guarantees success, and no combination of scores that guarantees failure. As a rough guide: if most signals are consistently low, reconsider this particular market rather than forcing it. If you have a mix — one or two strong signals alongside a weak one — go back and research that specific weak signal further before deciding; it's often fixable with more looking, not a dead end. If your signals are consistently medium-to-high across the board, you have enough to proceed to Module 2 with reasonable confidence.

When you're ready to score, open the Market Pulse Check below for each candidate market and set the four sliders using what you actually logged — not a general impression. If a slider value surprises you (say, you want to set Wallet to 8 but your log has no real spending evidence), that's a sign to go find more evidence before continuing, not to round up.
lessons.insight: The score isn't the point — the evidence behind it is. Two people can score the same market differently and both be right, if one has done five hours of research and the other five minutes.

signals.label: Hunger
signals.question: Do people genuinely want this problem solved?
signals.detail: Intensity of the customer's problem or desire.

signals.label: Wallet
signals.question: Can this audience realistically pay for a solution?

signals.label: Reach
signals.question: Can you find and communicate with these people?

signals.label: Momentum
signals.question: Is the demand stable, emerging or growing?
signals.detail: Direction and opportunity of the market.

exercise.instructions: Evaluate up to three potential markets using the four signals, based on the evidence you logged in Lesson 1.2. Your highest-scoring option becomes your Target Customer Profile.

prompts.title: Market Research Prompt
prompts.purpose: Use this to pressure-test your market idea before committing to it.
prompts.template: You are a customer-acquisition strategist helping someone pick a specific, well-matched niche, not a vague demographic. My skill or expertise: {{m0.path}}. Candidate niches I'm considering: {{m1.marketNames}}. Score each candidate against DigitalOps's Market Pulse Check — Hunger (real pain), Wallet (spending power), Reach (easy to find them), and Momentum (a growing market). Tell me which one scores highest and why. If I haven't given you enough detail on any candidate to score it fairly, tell me exactly what's missing and ask me for it before scoring. If any niche I've picked sounds like "everyone" or is too broad to target with one message, say so plainly instead of scoring it as-is. Return a short table (Niche | Pain | Spending power | Reach | Growth | Verdict) plus two sentences on your top pick. Don't invent market-size numbers or cite research that doesn't exist — reason only from what I've given you and ordinary common sense.

prompts.title: Market Discovery Prompt
prompts.purpose: Use this first, before scoring, to find out where your audience already talks.
prompts.template: You are a market-research strategist helping someone find out where their potential audience already discusses relevant problems — not someone evaluating ideas they've already picked. My expertise or starting point: {{m0.path}}. My candidate market(s) so far: {{m1.marketNames}}. Suggest 3 to 5 specific, real kinds of places (name actual community types — particular subreddits, forum categories, marketplace sections, app categories) where this audience is likely already talking about problems in this space, and give two example search phrases I could adapt for each one. Then tell me what kind of evidence to look for once I'm there (recurring complaints, workarounds people already use, signs they're paying for something adjacent), and flag one research blind spot — a type of venue I've likely overlooked given my market. If my expertise or candidate market above is too vague to suggest real venues, tell me what's missing and ask before guessing. Everything you suggest is a place to go verify, not a confirmed finding — present it that way, and never invent specific community names, customer quotes, or statistics you aren't reasonably confident are real.
